November 4, 20263:24 PM ET

Adam Burke
Lilien Begay, 92, seated at left with daughters (clockwise) Berneice, Darlene, and Vera at the voting site in Denehotso, Arizona on Nov. 3, 2026
Adam Burke/KSUT
hide caption
toggle caption i
Adam Burke/KSUT
People on the Navajo Reservation had to make extra effort to vote this year.
It's a region of the southwest that's been hit this fall by repeated flooding. Roads washed out, driving thousands of people from their homes.
But voters turned out, in the parts of Arizona, Utah and New Mexico that the reservation stretches across. Yesterday at the Dennehotso Chapterhouse, voters rolled up in trucks with mud-caked tires.
The town is framed by the picturesque sandstone cursive of Comb Ridge, the stone spires of Monument Valley peeking over the ridgeline.
In the parking lot, people gathered to eat fry bread and mutton stew, something common at Navajo polling sites.
"I love to see our people come out and talk amongst each other," said 27-year-old Urbina Yazzie, adding that this year's election is unusual.
"People are having to drive on tractors to get from one road to another, just to come and vote," she said.

item.title: Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
item.description:
Obituaries
Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
November 4, 20263:11 PM ET
Tom Huizenga
Herbert Blomstedt conducts the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig in April 2026, at the age of 98.
Jan Woitas/picture alliance/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Jan Woitas/picture alliance/Getty Images
Herbert Blomstedt, an American-born, Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him leading many of the world's major orchestras, including the San Francisco Symphony for 10 years, died on Wednesday at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden. He was 99.
His death was announced in a statement released by his management company, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.
In a profession routinely flush with elderly practitioners, Blomstedt, year after year, retained his title as the world's oldest active conductor. He worked into his late 90s, conducting concerts this year, at the age of 98, with the Detroit Symphony and the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, Germany.
"Retirement is not a question of age," Blomstedt told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. "It should be flexible. I just love the music so much that I just can't give up." And he didn't.

Jacquelyn Martin/AP

Jacquelyn Martin/AP
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
After a bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.
The Louisiana Republican served two terms as speaker, elected after his predecessor, California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, was ousted in 2023.
Johnson's decision will open a role for the top House leadership position in the minority. Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10.
Historically, the president's party loses seats in midterm elections. The blue wave soared past the expectations of many in Washington, flipping seats in traditionally red states that the president has won previously.

Democrats won big in the midterm elections, but with President Trump still in the White House, the next Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law.
Instead, expect to see a lot more oversight. With public corruption and failing leadership as two of the top issues concerning voters, congressional Democrats have an ambitious agenda of investigations planned for their return to power in the House and Senate.
Their new majorities mean that they will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records for review and compel individuals to testify before lawmakers.

item.title: The world is reacting to the Democrats' sweeping midterm elections victory
item.description:

The world is reacting to the Democrats' sweeping midterm elections victory
Updated November 4, 20263:13 PM ET
Originally published November 4, 20267:34 AM ET
By
Kate Bartlett
The sun rises behind the Lincoln Memorial, lower left, Washington Monument and U.S. Capitol, in Washington, Wednesday, across the Potomac River from Arlington, Va.
Allison Robbert/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Allison Robbert/AP
One color dominates international headlines about the U.S. midterm election results. French newspaper Libération called the Democrats' win "une vague bleue," or blue wave, Britain's Daily Mail dubbed it a "historic blue tsunami," and The Times of India's headline ran "midterm blues for Trump."
Countries at war were also watching closely, with Ukrainian newspaper The Kyiv Independent's online headline hopeful: "Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine."
Russia had a different take. Rossiyskaya Gazeta, the state-run daily newspaper, suggested the results would in fact be a blow to Ukraine, which has firm support from the European Union. "Brussels, brace yourself. After the Republicans' defeat, Trump's wrath will fall on Europe," read the headline.
